stimuli.title: The Federalist No. 70 (1788)
stimuli.html:
Energy in the Executive is a leading character in the definition of good government. It is essential to the protection of the community against foreign attacks; it is not less essential to the steady administration of the laws; to the protection of property against those irregular and high-handed combinations which sometimes interrupt the ordinary course of justice; to the security of liberty against the enterprises and assaults of ambition, of faction, and of anarchy. . . .

A feeble Executive implies a feeble execution of the government. A feeble execution is but another phrase for a bad execution; and a government ill executed, whatever it may be in theory, must be, in practice, a bad government. . . .

The ingredients which constitute energy in the Executive are, first, unity; secondly, duration; thirdly, an adequate provision for its support; fourthly, competent powers. . . .

Decision, activity, secrecy, and dispatch will generally characterize the proceedings of one man in a much more eminent degree than the proceedings of any greater number; and in proportion as the number is increased, these qualities will be diminished.
stimuli.source: Excerpts from The Federalist No. 70, by Alexander Hamilton (published under the pen name "Publius"), March 1788; spelling modernized

stimuli.title: U.S. Constitution, Article IV (excerpts)
stimuli.html:
Section 1. Full Faith and Credit shall be given in each State to the public Acts, Records, and judicial Proceedings of every other State. . . .

Section 2. The Citizens of each State shall be entitled to all Privileges and Immunities of Citizens in the several States.

A Person charged in any State with Treason, Felony, or other Crime, who shall flee from Justice, and be found in another State, shall on Demand of the executive Authority of the State from which he fled, be delivered up, to be removed to the State having Jurisdiction of the Crime. . . .

Section 3. New States may be admitted by the Congress into this Union; but no new State shall be formed or erected within the Jurisdiction of any other State; nor any State be formed by the Junction of two or more States, or Parts of States, without the Consent of the Legislatures of the States concerned as well as of the Congress.

The Congress shall have Power to dispose of and make all needful Rules and Regulations respecting the Territory or other Property belonging to the United States . . .

Section 4. The United States shall guarantee to every State in this Union a Republican Form of Government, and shall protect each of them against Invasion; and on Application of the Legislature, or of the Executive (when the Legislature cannot be convened) against domestic Violence.
stimuli.source: Excerpts from the Constitution of the United States, Article IV (1787)

stimuli.title: States Formed from Parts of Other States
stimuli.html:
Four states were created from land that had been part of, or claimed by, an existing state. In each case, Congress voted to admit the new state.

stimuli.title: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819)
stimuli.html:
In 1816, Congress created the Second Bank of the United States. Maryland then passed a law taxing any bank in the state that had not been chartered by Maryland. James McCulloch, an officer of the national bank's Baltimore branch, refused to pay the tax. The Supreme Court decided the case unanimously in 1819. Chief Justice John Marshall wrote:

Let the end be legitimate, let it be within the scope of the constitution, and all means which are appropriate, which are plainly adapted to that end, which are not prohibited, but consist with the letter and spirit of the constitution, are constitutional. . . .

That the power to tax involves the power to destroy; that the power to destroy may defeat and render useless the power to create . . . are propositions not to be denied. . . .

The result is a conviction that the States have no power, by taxation or otherwise, to retard, impede, burden, or in any manner control, the operations of the constitutional laws enacted by Congress to carry into execution the powers vested in the general government.
stimuli.source: Excerpts from the opinion of Chief Justice John Marshall, McCulloch v. Maryland, U.S. Supreme Court, 1819

stimuli.title: Political Cartoon (described)
stimuli.html:
The cartoon shows a two-lane highway that splits at a fork. A figure labeled THE STATES stands at the fork holding a map. Above the road, a huge hand labeled FEDERAL HIGHWAY FUNDS dangles a heavy money bag over the left branch, where a road sign reads DRINKING AGE 21. The right branch is marked with a small sign reading YOUR CHOICE, and that road is full of potholes. Uncle Sam leans on a fence nearby, smiling, and says, "It's entirely up to you."

Background: In 1984, Congress passed the National Minimum Drinking Age Act. Under the law, a state that allowed people under 21 to buy alcohol would lose a portion of its federal highway funds. In South Dakota v. Dole (1987), the Supreme Court upheld the law. By 1988, every state had set its minimum age to buy alcohol at 21.
stimuli.source: Original cartoon description and background written for this test

stimuli.title: The Sherman Antitrust Act (1890)
stimuli.html:
Congress passed this law in 1890, and President Benjamin Harrison signed it on July 2, 1890.

Section 1. Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is hereby declared to be illegal. . . .

Section 2. Every person who shall monopolize, or attempt to monopolize, or combine or conspire with any other person or persons, to monopolize any part of the trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, shall be deemed guilty of a misdemeanor, and, on conviction thereof, shall be punished by fine not exceeding five thousand dollars, or by imprisonment not exceeding one year, or by both said punishments, in the discretion of the court.
stimuli.source: Excerpts from An Act to Protect Trade and Commerce Against Unlawful Restraints and Monopolies (Sherman Antitrust Act), July 2, 1890

stimuli.title: Who Enforces Competition Laws?
stimuli.html:
Congress writes the nation's antitrust laws, but other parts of the federal government put them into action.

The Antitrust Division of the U.S. Department of Justice investigates companies suspected of breaking these laws. It can file lawsuits in federal court and, for serious violations such as secret price-fixing, bring criminal charges. In 1914, Congress passed the Clayton Antitrust Act, which listed more specific business practices that are illegal, and the Federal Trade Commission Act, which created the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to stop unfair methods of competition.

The FTC is led by five commissioners. The President nominates each commissioner, and the Senate must confirm the nomination. Commissioners serve staggered seven-year terms, and no more than three of the five may belong to the same political party.

Federal judges decide whether a company has actually broken the law. A court may order a company to pay fines, to stop a practice, or even to split into separate companies. When two large competitors plan to merge, federal agencies may review the deal and ask a court to block it if they believe it would substantially lessen competition.
stimuli.source: Original reading written for this test

stimuli.title: The Antiquities Act (1906)
stimuli.html:
In the late 1800s and early 1900s, many people worried that ancient Native American dwellings and other historic sites on federal land in the West were being looted or destroyed. Congress responded with the Antiquities Act, which President Theodore Roosevelt signed on June 8, 1906. Section 2 reads in part:

That the President of the United States is hereby authorized, in his discretion, to declare by public proclamation historic landmarks, historic and prehistoric structures, and other objects of historic or scientific interest that are situated upon the lands owned or controlled by the Government of the United States to be national monuments, and may reserve as a part thereof parcels of land, the limits of which in all cases shall be confined to the smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects to be protected.

Roosevelt used the law to proclaim 18 national monuments. The first was Devils Tower in Wyoming (1906). Another was the Grand Canyon in Arizona (1908), which Congress later made a national park (1919).
stimuli.source: Excerpt from An Act for the Preservation of American Antiquities, June 8, 1906; background written for this test

stimuli.title: The Age of the Trusts
stimuli.html:
After the Civil War, railroads, oil, steel, and other industries grew rapidly. Some business leaders combined many companies into one giant organization called a trust. In 1882, John D. Rockefeller and his partners organized the Standard Oil Trust. By then, Standard Oil already controlled about 90 percent of the oil refining in the United States.

Trusts could cut costs and sometimes lower prices. But critics, including farmers, small business owners, and many journalists, charged that trusts crushed competitors, received secret discounts from railroads, and raised prices once rivals were gone. Several states passed their own antitrust laws, but a state law could not reach a trust that did business across the whole nation.

In 1890, Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act. At first, the law was rarely enforced. In 1895, in United States v. E. C. Knight Company, the Supreme Court ruled that manufacturing was not "commerce," so a company that controlled nearly all sugar refining in the country had not violated the act. Enforcement grew stronger under President Theodore Roosevelt, who became known as a "trust buster." In 1904, the Supreme Court ordered the breakup of the Northern Securities Company, which controlled major railroads in the Northwest. In 1911, the Court ordered Standard Oil split into 34 separate companies.
stimuli.source: Original reading written for this test

stimuli.title: Political Cartoon (described)
stimuli.html: This cartoon is drawn in the style of magazine cartoons of the 1880s. A gigantic octopus labeled THE TRUST sprawls across a map of the United States. Its long arms wrap around a railroad car, an oil refinery, a farmer's wagon, a state capitol building, and the dome of the U.S. Capitol in Washington. In the corner, a small man labeled THE PUBLIC holds a tiny pair of scissors labeled STATE LAWS and stares up at the creature. The caption asks, "Who Will Cut It Loose?"
stimuli.source: Original cartoon description written for this test

stimuli.title: The Great Society Address (1964)
stimuli.html:
President Lyndon B. Johnson gave this commencement address at the University of Michigan on May 22, 1964.

For in your time we have the opportunity to move not only toward the rich society and the powerful society, but upward to the Great Society.

The Great Society rests on abundance and liberty for all. It demands an end to poverty and racial injustice, to which we are totally committed in our time. But that is just the beginning. . . .

The challenge of the next half century is whether we have the wisdom to use that wealth to enrich and elevate our national life, and to advance the quality of our American civilization. . . .

So I want to talk to you today about three places where we begin to build the Great Society—in our cities, in our countryside, and in our classrooms.
stimuli.source: Excerpts from President Lyndon B. Johnson's remarks at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, May 22, 1964

stimuli.title: Selected Great Society Laws, 1964–1965
stimuli.html:

Economic Opportunity Act1964Created job-training and community programs, such as the Job Corps, as part of a "War on Poverty."
Wilderness Act1964Set up a system to protect large areas of federal land in their natural state.
Elementary and Secondary Education Act1965Gave federal money to public schools serving many children from low-income families.

stimuli.title: Competition and the Price of a Medicine
stimuli.html: When a company invents a new medicine, a patent usually gives it the sole right to sell that medicine for a number of years. After the patent expires, other companies may sell lower-cost copies, called generic versions. The graph shows how the average price of a 30-day supply of one medicine changed as the number of companies selling it grew.

stimuli.html: The graph shows the share of all energy used in the United States in 2024 that came from each source. Renewable energy includes hydroelectric power, wind, solar, wood and other biomass, and geothermal energy.

stimuli.title: Energy and Geography
stimuli.html:
Energy resources are not spread evenly across the United States. Where a resource is found shapes how people use the land around it.

Texas produces more crude oil and natural gas than any other state. Wyoming produces more coal than any other state, most of it from huge surface mines in the Powder River Basin. Coal, oil, and natural gas are fossil fuels: they formed over millions of years, and once they are burned they cannot be replaced on any human time scale.

Renewable resources depend on climate and landforms. The flat, open Great Plains, stretching from Texas north to the Dakotas, have strong and steady winds, so wind turbines now dot much of the region; Texas generates more electricity from wind than any other state. The sunny, dry Southwest is well suited to solar power. In the Pacific Northwest, the Columbia River carries an enormous volume of water and drops steeply on its way to the Pacific Ocean. Dozens of dams on the Columbia and its branches make Washington the nation's leading producer of hydroelectric power.

Cheap electricity from these dams attracted industries that use huge amounts of power. Beginning in the 1940s, several aluminum plants were built along the Columbia, because making aluminum requires enormous amounts of electricity. Dams also brought costs. They blocked the paths of salmon, which swim upriver to lay their eggs, and many salmon runs declined sharply. Builders added fish ladders—stair-step channels of water—to help some fish pass the dams, but salmon populations remain far below their historic levels.
stimuli.source: Original reading written for this test; facts from the U.S. Energy Information Administration

items.skill: Civics: main idea of a primary source
items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Hamilton's main argument in the excerpt?
options: A strong, energetic executive is necessary for good government.
The executive should be weaker than the legislature so that it cannot threaten liberty.
Executive power should be shared by a council of several leaders.
A government will work well in practice as long as its written plan is good in theory.
items.explain: Hamilton opens by calling "Energy in the Executive" a leading feature "of good government" and warns that "a feeble Executive implies a feeble execution of the government." His main point is that the executive must be strong and energetic. The last choice reverses his claim: he says a government that is poorly carried out is bad "whatever it may be in theory." He also argues that energy declines as the number of leaders increases, so he would oppose a council.

items.skill: Civics: structure of the executive branch
items.prompt: Hamilton names "unity" as the first ingredient of energy in the executive. Which feature of the Constitution best reflects this idea?
options: Congress is divided into two houses.
The executive power is placed in one President.
Federal judges serve during good behavior.
The Senate must approve treaties by a two-thirds vote.
items.explain: By "unity," Hamilton means a single person rather than a group. He argues that "decision, activity, secrecy, and dispatch" are found in "one man" more than in "any greater number." Article II reflects this: "The executive Power shall be vested in a President of the United States of America." A two-house Congress and Senate approval of treaties do the opposite: they divide and share power. Terms of federal judges concern the judicial branch, not the executive.

items.skill: Civics: point of view and historical context
items.prompt:
Complete the statement.

Hamilton wrote The Federalist essays to persuade New Yorkers to {{0}} the proposed Constitution. His defense of a strong executive answered the {{1}}, who warned that a powerful President might come to resemble {{2}}.

options: ratify
reject
delay
rewrite
Federalists
Loyalists
Anti-Federalists
Whigs
a British king
a Supreme Court justice
a state governor
a town council

items.explain: The Federalist essays were published in New York newspapers in 1787–1788 to win support for ratifying the Constitution. Their opponents, the Anti-Federalists, feared that a single powerful executive would act like a British king—the kind of ruler the colonists had just rejected. The Federalists were Hamilton's own side, so they were not the critics he was answering. Loyalists had sided with Britain during the Revolution and were not the main opponents of ratification.

items.prompt: A court in Ohio orders a man to pay $8,000 that he owes a contractor. Before paying, the man moves to Indiana. The contractor asks an Indiana court to enforce the Ohio court's decision. Which part of Article IV most directly requires Indiana to respect the Ohio decision?
options: Section 2, the Privileges and Immunities Clause
Section 3, the clause on admitting new states
Section 1, the Full Faith and Credit Clause
Section 4, the guarantee of a republican form of government
items.explain: Section 1 says "Full Faith and Credit shall be given in each State to the public Acts, Records, and judicial Proceedings of every other State." A court judgment is a judicial proceeding, so Indiana must honor it. The Privileges and Immunities Clause protects citizens from being treated unfairly when they are in another state; it does not deal with enforcing court decisions. Sections 3 and 4 concern new states and forms of government.

items.prompt: A person charged with a felony in Georgia flees and is later found in South Carolina. According to Article IV, Section 2, what should happen?
options: South Carolina may try the person in its own courts for the Georgia crime.
The person may stay in South Carolina because the crime was committed in another state.
Congress must vote on whether to return the person to Georgia.
On demand of Georgia's executive authority, South Carolina must deliver the person to be returned to Georgia.
items.explain: Section 2 says a person charged with a crime who flees to another state "shall on Demand of the executive Authority of the State from which he fled, be delivered up, to be removed to the State having Jurisdiction of the Crime." Georgia's governor (its executive authority) makes the demand, and the person is returned to Georgia, where the crime happened. This process is called extradition. The clause gives the decision to the states' executives, not to Congress, and it sends the case back to the state with jurisdiction rather than letting South Carolina try it.

items.prompt: Drag each situation into the part of Article IV that most directly applies to it.
choices: A birth certificate issued in Texas is accepted as valid in Oregon.
Tennessee may not bar a Georgia resident from owning property in Tennessee simply because she lives in Georgia.
Congress votes to admit a territory as a new state.
A state that tried to replace its elected legislature with a hereditary ruler would violate the Constitution.
A child-custody order issued by a court in one state is enforced by a court in another state.
items.explain: Full Faith and Credit: a Texas birth certificate accepted in Oregon, and a child-custody order from one state's court enforced in another, are both "public Records" or "judicial Proceedings" honored across state lines. Privileges and Immunities: a state may not deny a Georgia resident the right to own property in Tennessee just because of where she lives; citizens of each state share the basic privileges of citizens in other states. New States: Congress admits new states under Section 3. Republican Government: a hereditary ruler would replace government by elected representatives, which Section 4 guarantees to every state. A common mistake is putting the property example under Full Faith and Credit; that clause is about honoring another state's laws, records, and court decisions, not about how a state treats visitors.

items.prompt: According to Article IV, Section 4, under what condition will the United States protect a state against "domestic Violence"?
options: When the state's legislature, or its executive if the legislature cannot meet, asks for help
Whenever the President decides on his or her own that a riot is taking place
Only after Congress has declared war
When a majority of the other states vote to send aid
items.explain: Section 4 promises protection against domestic violence "on Application of the Legislature, or of the Executive (when the Legislature cannot be convened)." In other words, the state must ask. Protection against invasion is promised without any request, which may be why some readers choose the second option, but the excerpt attaches the request requirement to domestic violence. Nothing in the section mentions a declaration of war or a vote of the other states.

items.skill: Civics: interpreting a table and a document
items.prompt: Based on Article IV, Section 3, and the table, why was the consent of Massachusetts' legislature needed before Maine could become a state?
options: Every new state must be approved by the legislatures of all existing states.
Maine was being formed within the jurisdiction of an existing state.
Massachusetts had to write Maine's state constitution.
The President could not sign a statehood law without a state's approval.
items.explain: Section 3 says no new state may be "formed or erected within the Jurisdiction of any other State" without "the Consent of the Legislatures of the States concerned as well as of the Congress." The table shows Maine was formed from Massachusetts, so Massachusetts was the state concerned, and its legislature consented in 1819. Only the state or states concerned must agree, not every state, so the first choice is wrong. The table shows the same pattern for Kentucky and West Virginia, which were formed from Virginia.

items.prompt: Which idea is expressed in Chief Justice Marshall's statement beginning "Let the end be legitimate"?
options: Congress may use only the powers that are specifically listed in the Constitution.
States may refuse to follow federal laws they believe are unconstitutional.
Congress may use reasonable means not listed in the Constitution to carry out its constitutional goals.
The Supreme Court must approve every law before it takes effect.
items.explain: Marshall says that if the goal ("the end") is within the Constitution's scope, then any "appropriate" means that are "plainly adapted to that end" and not prohibited are constitutional. This is the doctrine of implied powers, based on the Necessary and Proper Clause. Creating a bank is not a listed power, but it helps Congress carry out listed powers such as taxing and borrowing. The first choice describes the strict reading of the Constitution that Marshall rejected.

items.prompt: What did Marshall mean when he wrote that "the power to tax involves the power to destroy"?
options: Congress should not be allowed to tax banks of any kind.
All taxes harm the economy and should be kept as low as possible.
The national government may destroy any state bank that competes with the national bank.
If a state could tax a federal institution, it could use that tax to weaken or even destroy the institution.
items.explain: Marshall's point is that a tax can be set so high that it ruins what is taxed. If Maryland could tax the national bank, it could use taxes to drive the bank out of business and "defeat" what Congress lawfully created. That is why he concludes that states have no power "by taxation or otherwise" to "burden, or in any manner control" federal laws. The ruling limited state taxing of federal institutions; it did not say all taxes are harmful or that Congress may destroy state banks.

items.prompt: Which principles did the Supreme Court support in McCulloch v. Maryland? Select two answers.
options: Congress has implied powers beyond those listed in the Constitution.
Valid federal laws are supreme over state laws that conflict with them.
The power of judicial review was first established in this case.
States may tax federal institutions as long as the tax rate is low.
The Tenth Amendment limits Congress to its expressly listed powers.
items.explain: The Court held that Congress has implied powers (it could create a bank as a means to carry out listed powers) and that valid federal laws are supreme over state laws that conflict with them (Maryland could not tax or "control" the bank). Judicial review was established earlier, in Marbury v. Madison (1803), so it was not first established here. The Court said states may not tax federal institutions at all, whatever the rate, and it rejected the idea that Congress is limited to its expressly listed powers.

items.prompt: What is the main message of the cartoon?
options: The federal government can use money to pressure states into adopting policies that the states officially control.
States should spend more of their own money repairing roads.
The Constitution requires every state to set its drinking age at 21.
Most states asked Congress to set a national drinking age.
items.explain: Uncle Sam says the choice is "entirely up to you," but the money bag hangs over the DRINKING AGE 21 road and the other road is full of potholes. The cartoonist is pointing out that the "choice" comes with a heavy financial pressure. The background confirms that Congress did not order states to change the drinking age; it withheld highway funds from states that did not. That is why the third choice is wrong: no part of the Constitution sets a drinking age.

items.skill: Civics: federalism and the spending power
items.prompt:
Complete the statement.

Setting the minimum age to buy alcohol is generally a power {{0}}. Instead of ordering states to change their laws, Congress used its power to {{1}} to encourage them to act. In South Dakota v. Dole, the Supreme Court {{2}} this approach.

options: delegated only to Congress
reserved to the states
given to the President
held by federal courts
admit new states
regulate the value of money
declare war
spend money for the general welfare
struck down
refused to hear
upheld

items.explain: Alcohol laws such as the drinking age are reserved to the states; the Constitution does not give Congress a power to set them directly. Congress instead relied on its power to spend money for the general welfare, attaching a condition to highway grants. According to the background, the Supreme Court upheld the law. Regulating the value of money and admitting new states are real powers of Congress, but neither relates to highway grants.

items.skill: Civics: constitutional basis of a law
items.prompt: On which power of Congress did the Sherman Antitrust Act most directly rely?
options: The power to coin money and regulate its value
The power to regulate commerce among the states and with foreign nations
The power to admit new states into the Union
The power to establish post offices and post roads
items.explain: Both sections of the act apply to "trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations." That wording matches the Commerce Clause of Article I, Section 8, which gives Congress power "to regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States." The act does not deal with money, new states, or the mail.

items.prompt: Which action would most clearly violate Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act?
options: A bakery lowers its prices to win customers from a nearby rival.
A small software company becomes the market leader because customers prefer its product.
The three largest cement makers in a region secretly agree to charge the same high price.
Two neighboring hardware stores compete by staying open later.
items.explain: Section 1 makes illegal "every contract, combination . . . or conspiracy, in restraint of trade." A secret agreement among competitors to set the same high price (price-fixing) is a conspiracy that restrains trade. Lowering prices or staying open later is ordinary competition. A company that wins customers with a better product has not made any agreement with others, and simply becoming the leader is not illegal; Section 2 targets efforts to monopolize, not success alone.

items.prompt: Drag each action into the branch of the federal government that carries it out.
choices: Passes the Sherman Antitrust Act
The Department of Justice files a lawsuit to block a merger
Orders a company to split into separate companies
Confirms the President's nominee to the Federal Trade Commission
Nominates a commissioner to the Federal Trade Commission
Decides whether a company broke the antitrust laws
items.explain: Legislative (Congress): passing antitrust laws such as the Sherman Act, and the Senate's confirmation of FTC commissioners. Executive: the President's nomination of commissioners and the Department of Justice's lawsuits; the Justice Department is an executive department. Judicial: federal judges decide whether a company broke the law and may order it split up. A common mistake is placing the Justice Department's lawsuit in the judicial branch because it happens in court; the department brings the case, but the court decides it.

items.skill: Civics: purpose of a government rule
items.prompt: The reading states that no more than three of the five FTC commissioners may belong to the same political party. This rule is most likely intended to
options: allow the President to remove commissioners who disagree with him or her.
make sure each commissioner serves exactly seven years.
give the Senate control over the FTC's daily decisions.
keep a single political party from fully controlling the commission's decisions.
items.explain: If no more than three commissioners can belong to one party, at least two seats must go to people outside that party. This builds in balance so that the commission's decisions are not controlled entirely by one party. The rule says nothing about removal, term length (the seven-year terms are a separate rule), or Senate control of day-to-day work; the Senate's role is to confirm nominees.

items.prompt: Article IV, Section 3, gives Congress the power to "make all needful Rules and Regulations respecting the Territory or other Property belonging to the United States." Which statement best describes how the Antiquities Act relates to this power?
options: Congress used its power over federal property to pass a law allowing the President to protect certain federal lands.
The President created a new power without any law passed by Congress.
The act transferred ownership of federal land to the states where it was located.
The act is an example of a state using its reserved powers to protect land.
items.explain: The Antiquities Act is a law passed by Congress, and it covers only objects "situated upon the lands owned or controlled by the Government of the United States"—federal property, which Article IV places under Congress's authority. Through the act, Congress gave (delegated) to the President the power to proclaim national monuments. The second choice is wrong because the President's power comes from the act itself: "the President . . . is hereby authorized." The act kept the land federal and was a national law, not a state action.

items.prompt: Based on the excerpt, the Antiquities Act gave the President the power to
options: buy private land from landowners to create new parks.
set aside federal land as national monuments to protect objects of historic or scientific interest.
create national parks without any further action by Congress.
fine anyone who damaged a historic site on private property.
items.explain: The act authorizes the President "to declare by public proclamation . . . objects of historic or scientific interest that are situated upon the lands owned or controlled by the Government of the United States to be national monuments." The background shows the difference between a monument and a park: Roosevelt proclaimed the Grand Canyon a national monument in 1908, but it was Congress that made it a national park in 1919. The act applies to land the government already owns or controls, not to buying private land.

items.prompt: The Antiquities Act is most closely connected to which movement of the early 1900s?
options: The abolition movement
The temperance movement
The conservation movement
The labor union movement
items.explain: The act was a response to the looting and destruction of historic sites, and it let the President protect natural and historic places on federal land. Protecting land and resources for the future was the goal of the conservation movement, which President Theodore Roosevelt strongly supported. The abolition movement had ended slavery decades earlier, temperance focused on limiting alcohol, and labor unions focused on workers' wages and conditions.

items.prompt: According to the reading, why was a national antitrust law needed in addition to state laws?
options: The Supreme Court had struck down every state antitrust law.
Trusts had stopped lowering prices for consumers in every state.
State governments had asked Congress to break up Standard Oil immediately.
A single state's law could not effectively control a trust that did business across the whole nation.
items.explain: The reading says, "Several states passed their own antitrust laws, but a state law could not reach a trust that did business across the whole nation." Then Congress passed the Sherman Act. The reading never says the Supreme Court struck down state laws; the 1895 Court decision it mentions limited the federal act. It also says trusts could "sometimes lower prices," so the second choice is not supported.

items.prompt: Using the reading, place these turning points in the federal fight against trusts on a timeline. Drag the oldest one into the 1st box and the most recent into the 5th box.
choices: Supreme Court orders Northern Securities Company broken up
Standard Oil Trust is organized
Supreme Court orders Standard Oil split into 34 companies
Congress passes the Sherman Antitrust Act
Supreme Court rules in E. C. Knight that manufacturing is not commerce
items.explain: Correct order: (1) Standard Oil Trust organized, 1882; (2) Sherman Antitrust Act passed, 1890; (3) E. C. Knight decision limits the act, 1895; (4) Northern Securities Company broken up, 1904; (5) Standard Oil split into 34 companies, 1911. A common mistake is placing the Standard Oil breakup before Northern Securities because Standard Oil appears first in the reading; the breakup came seven years later.

items.skill: U.S. history: interpreting a political cartoon
items.prompt: Which statement best describes the cartoonist's point of view?
options: Trusts had grown so powerful that they controlled business and government, and state laws were too weak to stop them.
Trusts were helping farmers and railroads work together more efficiently.
State antitrust laws were strong enough to control the trusts.
The federal government was the main cause of the trusts' growth.
items.explain: The octopus's arms wrap around industries (railroads, oil), farmers, and even government buildings (a state capitol and the U.S. Capitol), showing that the trust has a grip on both the economy and politics. The tiny scissors labeled STATE LAWS show that the public's tool is far too small for the job, and the caption asks who can cut the creature loose. This matches the reading's point that state laws could not reach national trusts. The cartoon shows the trust as a threat, not a helper.

items.skill: U.S. history: main idea of a speech
items.prompt: What is Johnson's main purpose in the excerpt?
options: To announce that poverty in the United States had already been ended
To call on Americans to use the nation's wealth to end poverty and injustice and improve the quality of American life
To argue that the nation should focus mainly on increasing its military power
To explain why the federal government should reduce its role in education
items.explain: Johnson says the Great Society "demands an end to poverty and racial injustice" and asks whether the nation has "the wisdom to use that wealth to enrich and elevate our national life." His purpose is to call the country toward these goals. He says this is "just the beginning," so poverty had clearly not been ended. He contrasts the Great Society with merely "the powerful society," so military strength is not his focus, and he names classrooms as a place to build the Great Society.

items.prompt: Johnson said the Great Society "demands an end to poverty and racial injustice." Which laws in the table were aimed most directly at ending racial injustice? Select two answers.
options: Civil Rights Act (1964)
Wilderness Act (1964)
Economic Opportunity Act (1964)
Voting Rights Act (1965)
Elementary and Secondary Education Act (1965)
items.explain: The Civil Rights Act outlawed segregation in public places and banned job discrimination based on race, and the Voting Rights Act banned literacy tests that had been used to keep Black citizens from voting. The Economic Opportunity Act and the Elementary and Secondary Education Act targeted poverty, and the Wilderness Act protected land. These laws address other Great Society goals, but not racial injustice as directly.

items.prompt: Which statement about the Great Society is a fact rather than an opinion?
options: The Great Society was the most important set of reforms in American history.
Medicare is the best possible way to provide health care for older Americans.
The Social Security Amendments of 1965 created Medicare and Medicaid.
Johnson's speech at the University of Michigan was the finest address of his presidency.
items.explain: A fact can be checked and proved true. The table shows that the Social Security Amendments of 1965 created Medicare and Medicaid, and that can be verified in the law itself. The other statements use judgment words—"most important," "best possible," "finest"—that express a personal view people could reasonably disagree about.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
options: The price of the medicine rose as more companies began selling it.
The price stayed about the same until eight companies were selling it.
The price fell only when the second company entered the market.
The average price fell as the number of companies selling the medicine increased.
items.explain: Read the bars from left to right: $240 (1 seller), $204 (2), $150 (3), $96 (5), $60 (8). Each time more sellers entered, the average price was lower. This shows how competition tends to push prices down. The price did fall when the second company entered ($240 to $204), but it kept falling after that, so the third choice is wrong.

items.prompt: By what percent did the average price fall from when there was 1 seller to when there were 5 sellers?
items.explain:
Price with 1 seller: $240. Price with 5 sellers: $96.
Decrease: 240 − 96 = 144.
Percent decrease: 144 ÷ 240 = 0.6 = 60 percent.
A common error is dividing by the new price (144 ÷ 96 = 1.5, or 150%); percent change is always measured from the starting value.

items.skill: Economics: monopoly and barriers to entry
items.prompt:
Complete the statement.

While the patent is in effect, its maker is the only company allowed to sell the medicine, so the market is a {{0}}. The patent acts as a {{1}} that keeps other companies out. Compared with a market with many sellers, a company in this position can usually charge {{2}} prices.

options: oligopoly
monopoly
perfectly competitive market
barter economy
subsidy
price ceiling
barrier to entry
tariff
higher
lower
identical

items.explain: A market with a single seller and no close substitutes is a monopoly. A patent is a legal barrier to entry: other firms are not allowed to enter and compete until it expires. Without competitors, the seller can charge higher prices, as the $240 price with one seller shows. An oligopoly has a few sellers, not one. A price ceiling is a government limit on prices, which would push prices down, not keep competitors out.

items.prompt: Markets differ in how many sellers compete in them. Drag each example into the market structure it best represents.
choices: The only company allowed to deliver tap water in a city
Hundreds of farmers selling identical corn at a grain market
Two companies that build nearly all of the world's large passenger jets
Dozens of food trucks competing for lunch customers downtown
A handful of national companies that provide most U.S. cell phone service
The only bridge across a wide river, owned by one company that charges a toll
items.explain: Monopoly (one seller): the only company allowed to deliver tap water in a city, and the only toll bridge across a wide river; customers have no close substitute. Oligopoly (a few large sellers): the two companies that build nearly all large passenger jets, and the handful of national companies that provide most cell phone service. Many competing sellers: hundreds of farmers selling identical corn, and dozens of food trucks. A common mistake is putting the cell phone companies under monopoly; there is more than one, but only a few, so it is an oligopoly.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
options: Fossil fuels (petroleum, natural gas, and coal) supplied more than 80 percent of U.S. energy in 2024.
Renewable energy supplied more of the nation's energy than nuclear power did.
Coal was the largest single source of U.S. energy in 2024.
Natural gas supplied more of the nation's energy than petroleum did.
items.explain: Add the fossil fuel bars: 38 + 36 + 8 = 82 percent, which is more than 80 percent. Renewable energy and nuclear power were equal (9 percent each), so the second choice is wrong. Coal was the smallest source shown (8 percent), and natural gas (36 percent) was slightly below petroleum (38 percent).

items.prompt: What percent of U.S. energy in 2024 came from petroleum and natural gas combined?
items.explain:
Petroleum: 38 percent. Natural gas: 36 percent.
38 + 36 = 74 percent.
A common error is adding coal as well (38 + 36 + 8 = 82); the question asks only about petroleum and natural gas.

items.prompt: According to the reading, which feature of the Pacific Northwest best explains why Washington leads the nation in hydroelectric power?
options: Strong, steady winds blow across flat, open land.
A large river carries a huge volume of water and drops steeply toward the ocean.
Huge surface mines produce large amounts of coal.
The climate is sunny and dry for most of the year.
items.explain: Hydroelectric power uses falling or flowing water to spin turbines. The reading says the Columbia River "carries an enormous volume of water and drops steeply," and dozens of dams on it make Washington the leading producer. Strong winds over flat land describe the Great Plains (wind power), surface coal mines describe Wyoming, and a sunny, dry climate describes the Southwest (solar power).

items.prompt: Based on the reading, which statement best explains why aluminum plants were built along the Columbia River beginning in the 1940s?
options: The Columbia River region had the nation's largest deposits of coal for running the plants.
Salmon fishing created a large workforce that needed new jobs.
Making aluminum requires enormous amounts of electricity, which the dams supplied at low cost.
Fish ladders made it easier to ship aluminum by river.
items.explain: The reading says that "cheap electricity from these dams attracted industries that use huge amounts of power" and that aluminum plants were built "because making aluminum requires enormous amounts of electricity." This is an example of how a region's natural resources shape where industries locate. The leading coal state named in the reading is Wyoming, not a state on the Columbia, and fish ladders help salmon pass dams; they have nothing to do with shipping.

items.prompt: A region is considering building a new dam on a river where salmon swim upstream to lay their eggs. Based on the reading, which statement best describes the main trade-off?
options: The dam would supply fossil fuel energy but would lower the price of electricity.
The dam would create jobs in coal mining but would reduce wind power.
The dam would increase salmon populations but would raise electricity prices.
The dam would produce renewable electricity but could block salmon from reaching the places where they lay their eggs.
items.explain: The reading describes both sides of dams on the Columbia: they produce hydroelectric power, a renewable resource, and cheap electricity, but they "blocked the paths of salmon," and many salmon runs declined even with fish ladders. A trade-off means gaining one benefit at the cost of another. Hydroelectric power is renewable, not a fossil fuel, and the reading shows dams reduced salmon populations, so the first and third choices are wrong.
